title: How Should a Christian Think About Politics?
subtitle: How a Christian belongs to two kingdoms at once, the idolatry of the nation, the ancient church that worshiped a crucified Lord under a hostile empire, and what it means to engage as a citizen without selling your soul to a party. Refusing the captivity of the faith to either tribe while still loving your country and your neighbor.

parts.title: The God Who Fits on a Yard Sign
parts.body:
Watch what happens to your body when the other side wins an election. The drop in the stomach, the dread that feels almost spiritual, the sense that something sacred has been violated and that the world itself is now unsafe. Watch, too, what happens when your side wins, the surge of vindication, the feeling that righteousness has been restored, that the country has been saved. These are not the responses of a citizen exercising a vote. They are the responses of a worshiper whose god has been threatened or enthroned. And most of us, if we are honest, recognize the feeling.

Something has happened to the American believer, and it happened so gradually that few of us felt it occur. Politics stopped being one arena of life and became the arena, the lens through which everything else is now sorted, the thing that tells us who our friends are, what news is true, which Christians are sound, and whether the future is hope or catastrophe. We did not decide to make a kingdom of this world ultimate. We absorbed it, the way you absorb a fever, and now a political identity sits where a religious one used to be, often wearing its clothes.

Here is the symptom that should alarm us. For many believers, the tribe now reads the Bible, instead of the Bible reading the tribe. We can tell, before a Christian opens his mouth on any subject, what he will say, because we already know how he votes, and the politics has become the thing that is fixed while the faith bends to fit it. We have, without quite noticing, allowed the parties to disciple us. They got there first. They are more present, more emotionally insistent, more constant in our ears than the slow voice of Scripture, and they have shaped our reflexes while the sermon shaped only our opinions.

The believer caught in this knows something is wrong but cannot find the exit, because both tribes offer the same trap dressed in opposite colors. Each says that the kingdom of God depends on the right election, that the enemy is the other party, that faithfulness means total enlistment, and that any Christian who will not fully enlist is naive or compromised. The pressure comes from both sides, and it is the same pressure. Give us your ultimate allegiance. Let your hope and your fear be set by us. Make the nation, or the cause, the thing you would die for.

The ancient church had a one-sentence creed that got Christians killed, and it was a political sentence. Jesus is Lord. The reason it was deadly is that it ended with three unspoken words everyone understood. And Caesar is not.

parts.title: What Political Idolatry Costs
parts.body:
The first cost is to worship itself, because the human heart was built to give ultimate allegiance to something, and when it withdraws that allegiance from God it does not become neutral. It re-attaches. The political theorist and the prophet agree on this, that politics abhors a vacuum and rushes to fill the space that faith vacates, offering a god you can vote for, a salvation you can legislate, an enemy you can hate with a clear conscience, and a community of the righteous you can belong to. What looks like passionate citizenship is often displaced religion, and a displaced religion is an idol, and an idol always, the prophets warn, ends by demanding what only God may have.

The second cost is to the church's unity, which Jesus prayed for as the proof of his mission. The dividing line in the American church now is rarely doctrine. It is politics, and congregations split, friendships end, and believers leave not over the deity of Christ but over a candidate. We have allowed the parties to do to the body of Christ what no heresy could, to tear apart what the blood of Christ joined, so that the world looks at the church and sees not a new humanity but the same partisan war with worship music. When the tribe is thicker than the baptism, the church has already lost the argument it most needed to win.

The third cost is to the witness, and it may be the gravest. The watching skeptic has concluded, with painful evidence, that for many Christians the faith is a subset of the politics rather than the other way around, that the gospel is a flag the party flies, that the name of Jesus has become a tool in a power struggle. He has heard believers excuse in their own side what they condemn in the other, and he has drawn the obvious conclusion, that the morality was never the point, the tribe was. Every time the church baptizes a party's sins to win a party's battles, it tells the world that Jesus is for sale, and the world has been buying that conclusion in bulk.

And the fourth cost is to the soul of the believer, and here I have to speak about myself. Political idolatry hardens the heart it captures. It teaches you to feel righteous about your contempt, to receive comfortable lies because they serve your side, to fear the future as though God were not on the throne, and to love the people who agree with you while writing off the people who do not. I have felt the pull of all of it, the satisfaction of the dunk, the warmth of the tribe, the dread when my side loses, the suspicion that a brother who votes differently must be less than a brother. None of that came from Christ. It came from a kingdom of this world that wanted my heart, and got more of it than I knew.

parts.title: Two Kingdoms and One Lord
parts.body:
The Bible's vision begins with a claim that relativizes every government on earth. The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof. There is no authority except from God, Paul writes, which means every king, president, and party holds whatever power it has on loan, accountable to a throne above its own. This is the root of all Christian political sanity. No earthly kingdom is ultimate, because there is a kingdom over them all, and the believer's first citizenship, Paul says, is in heaven. We are, Peter writes, sojourners and exiles, resident aliens whose deepest loyalty lies elsewhere, and that single fact, held seriously, breaks the spell of every nation that asks to be worshiped.

Jesus himself drew the line with a precision the tribes keep blurring. When his enemies tried to trap him on the question of taxes, hoping he would either defy Rome or betray Israel, he asked whose image was on the coin, and when they said Caesar's, he said, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. The line is exact and devastating. Caesar may have his coin, his taxes, his real and limited authority. But the image on the coin is Caesar's, and the image on you is God's, and what bears God's image belongs to God alone. Caesar gets the coin. He does not get the worshiper. The whole of Christian political wisdom lives in that distinction.

When Jesus stood before Pilate, the line came clear again. My kingdom is not of this world, he said, for if it were, my servants would fight. He did not mean his kingdom has nothing to do with this world. He meant it does not run on this world's engine, which is force, the sword, the seizing of power. The kingdom of God advances by a cross, not a coup, by laid-down life rather than seized control, and a church that reaches for the sword to build it has confused its Lord with Caesar. The early Christians understood that they served a King who refused the very power their persecutors worshiped, and that the refusal was not weakness but the shape of the kingdom itself.

Yet the Bible never counsels withdrawal, and this is where it refuses the lazy options. The same Paul who calls us citizens of heaven submits to the governing authorities and uses his Roman citizenship to demand justice. The same prophets who relativize the nations command God's exiles in Babylon to seek the welfare of the city where they have been sent, to build houses, plant gardens, and pray for the peace of a pagan empire, because in its welfare they will find their own. The Christian is not an anarchist and not a hermit. He is a resident alien who loves the country he does not worship, works for its good, prays for its rulers, tells it the truth, and serves his neighbor through its common life, precisely because his hope is not riding on it.

And this is the freedom the gospel gives that no party can. Because the believer's ultimate hope is secured by a King already enthroned, he can engage in politics with energy and without idolatry, with conviction and without despair. He can lose an election without losing his world, because his world was never up for a vote. He can work hard for a just cause and still sleep at night, because the outcome rests finally in hands that were nailed for him and not in the hands of an electorate. He can love his political opponent as a neighbor rather than hate him as an enemy, because his security does not depend on defeating him. The Christian in the public square is meant to be the freest person there, owned by no tribe, terrified of no result, captive to no party, because he already belongs, body and soul, to the one Lord whose kingdom cannot be voted out.

parts.title: The Church Under Empire and the Long Temptation of Power
parts.body:
For its first three centuries the church had no political power at all, and it changed the world anyway. It was an illegal movement worshiping a man Rome had executed as a criminal, and its members refused the one act the empire required, the pinch of incense before the image of Caesar that said the state was lord. They would pay their taxes, pray for the emperor, and obey the laws, but they would not call him god, and for that refusal they were burned, fed to beasts, and crucified. Polycarp, the aged bishop, was told to swear by the fortune of Caesar and revile Christ, and answered that for eighty-six years Christ had done him no wrong and he could not blaspheme his King. He died for the distinction the tribes keep collapsing. Caesar gets the coin. He does not get the worship.

This powerless church produced a startling political theology. The Letter to Diognetus, written in the second century, described Christians as people who live in their own countries as resident aliens, who obey the established laws and yet surpass the laws in their own lives, who share all things as citizens and suffer all things as strangers. They were, it said, in the world what the soul is in the body, present everywhere, owned by nothing. They were the freest people in the empire because they feared the empire least, and their fearlessness in the face of death was itself a kind of testimony that the powers could not answer.

Then, in the fourth century, came the great reversal, and with it the long temptation. The emperor Constantine ended the persecution and the church moved from the catacombs to the palace. The gain was real, the end of the killing, the freedom to worship. But so was the danger, for the moment the church could hold the sword, it began to be tempted to use it, and the centuries that followed are a long, mixed record of a faith entangled with power. Augustine, watching Rome fall in 410, wrote the City of God to give the church a theology for exactly this, two cities woven together in history, the city of God built on the love of God and the earthly city built on the love of self, never to be identified with any nation, never fully separable until the end. He gave the church a way to live in an empire without worshiping it, and the church has needed that book ever since, because it keeps forgetting it.

The honest history is a warning written in both directions. The same church that stood fearless before Caesar later blessed crusades, burned dissenters, and crowned kings who claimed to rule by its God, confusing the kingdom of the cross with the kingdoms of the sword. And the same church, in other seasons, recovered the distinction at great cost. The Reformers wrestled hard with the two kingdoms. The Anabaptists paid in blood for insisting the church must never wield the state's sword. And in the twentieth century, when a German church largely surrendered to a nationalist idol and draped the cross in the flag of the Reich, a remnant in the Confessing Church wrote the Barmen Declaration in 1934, with Karl Barth's hand on the pen, refusing to let the state become the church's lord. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who paid for that refusal with his life in 1945, had seen exactly what happens when a church lets a nation become its god. The lesson of the whole history is one lesson, learned and forgotten and learned again. When the church marries the power of its age, it loses the gospel and gains a tomb. When it stays free, owned by Christ alone, it can speak the truth that the powers most need to hear and least want to.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: The relationship between religion, power, and the modern self is one of the most examined questions in political and social thought, and believers have nothing to fear from honest analysis of it. All truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every political theory carries a hidden picture of the human person, and the picture is where the argument lives.

secular.source: Political religion and the sacralizing of the state
secular.author: Eric Voegelin
secular.whatItGetsRight: Voegelin diagnosed the modern political mass movements as ersatz religions, attempts to build heaven on earth by political means once faith in a real heaven had drained away. He showed that the totalitarian movements of the twentieth century were not merely bad governments but substitute faiths, complete with their own eschatology, their own elect, and their own damned. He saw with terrible clarity that politics rushes to fill the space vacated by God.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Voegelin names the idol that Scripture named first, the kingdom of this world dressed as the kingdom of God, the tower of Babel reaching for heaven by human power. His analysis confirms the prophets, that the heart will worship something, and that a nation enthroned as god becomes a devourer. What he describes as a philosophical disorder, Scripture names as idolatry, with a personal God who is jealous for the worship being stolen, and a cross that breaks the spell no analysis alone can break.

secular.source: A Secular Age and the modern social imaginary
secular.author: Charles Taylor
secular.whatItGetsRight: Taylor traced how the West moved from a world where belief in God was nearly unavoidable to one where it is one option among many, and how the resulting buffered self seeks meaning and belonging in immanent things, the nation, the cause, the movement, that once pointed beyond themselves. He helps explain why politics now carries the emotional weight of religion for so many, including believers who imagine themselves immune.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Taylor maps the terrain that explains our political fevers, and Scripture supplies the older diagnosis underneath his account. The human person is, as Augustine said, made for God and restless until it rests in him, and the modern self that seeks ultimacy in politics is the restless heart looking for its rest in a kingdom that cannot bear the weight. Taylor describes the longing with rare subtlety. Scripture names its object, and offers the only rest that does not turn, in the end, into an idol that consumes its worshipers.

secular.source: The two cities and the limits of earthly politics
secular.author: Augustine of Hippo
secular.whatItGetsRight: Though a theologian, Augustine functions here as the West's most penetrating analyst of the relationship between faith and power, arguing that no earthly city can be identified with the kingdom of God, that every political order is a mixture of the love of God and the love of self, and that the believer must live in the earthly city as a pilgrim, using it without idolizing it. His realism punctures both the utopian who expects heaven from politics and the cynic who expects nothing.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Here the test is largely confirmation, for Augustine built his analysis on Scripture itself, on the citizenship in heaven and the call to seek the welfare of the city. The whole Bible holds the two truths he holds, that government is a real good ordained by God and that no government is the kingdom of God. If anything the caution Scripture adds is against the misuse of his two cities to justify Christian passivity, since the same God who relativizes the nations commands his people to seek their good and tell them the truth.

secular.source: Group polarization and the psychology of tribal politics
secular.author: Lilliana Mason and political scientists of identity
secular.whatItGetsRight: Mason and others demonstrated that American political identity has fused with social identity, so that party now functions like a tribe, sorting friends and enemies, generating contempt for outsiders, and bending people's beliefs to match their group rather than the other way around. They show, with data, exactly the dynamic Scripture assumes, that the heart follows the tribe and reasons backward to defend it.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The science confirms what the church should have known, that the tribe disciples the believer who does not resist it, bending his reading of even Scripture to fit his group. The Bible agrees the pull is powerful and calls the surrender to it a kind of slavery, for you are slaves of the one you obey. And it offers what the data cannot, a deeper belonging, the body of Christ across every tribe, and a Lord whose claim on the heart is meant to be stronger than the party's, so that the believer can be in a tribe without being owned by it.

secular.author: Benedict Anderson and the study of imagined communities
secular.whatItGetsRight: Anderson showed that the nation is an imagined community, a relatively modern construction that binds strangers into a single people willing to die and kill for one another, and that nationalism functions with the emotional and even sacred force of a religion, complete with martyrs, holy ground, and a promise of immortality through the collective. He explains the strange depth of devotion that flags and borders command.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Anderson exposes the nation as a powerful imagined fellowship, and Scripture both honors and relativizes it. The Bible affirms that peoples and nations are real and that loving one's own place and people is good, for God scattered the nations and set their boundaries. But it denies the nation the ultimacy nationalism claims, for the deepest community is not the imagined nation but the real and final one purchased from every tribe and tongue, a people whose immortality is not the survival of a flag but the resurrection of the dead. The nation may be loved. It may not be worshiped, and the gospel gives a belonging that outlasts every border.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who reject political idolatry and hold the same two-kingdoms vision still differ on how actively the church and the believer should engage the public square, and the difference is not careless. It runs to whether faithfulness calls for vigorous, world-shaping engagement in the institutions of power or for a quieter witness through a distinct and patient community. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are trying to serve one Lord and both are guarding against a real danger.

views.view: Engage the public square actively, seeking the good of the city through its institutions
views.body: This view holds that the command to seek the welfare of the city means Christians should be present and active in the institutions of public life, voting, advocating, serving in office, working through law and policy for justice and the common good. The model is Joseph and Daniel serving pagan governments with integrity, Paul using his citizenship, the prophets addressing kings. Advocates argue that to withdraw from politics is to abandon the neighbor to the mercy of those who do not love him, that government wields real power over real lives, and that a Christian who refuses to engage has confused holiness with absence. They insist that engagement can be done without idolatry, with a heart anchored in the kingdom of God and hands at work in the kingdoms of this world. The danger they are guarding against is a piety that keeps its robes clean by doing nothing, that lets injustice roll on while it congratulates itself on not being political, abandoning the public square to those who will fill it. Against that they hold that loving your neighbor in a society means caring about the laws and powers that shape his life, and that the resident alien is still commanded to build, plant, and seek the peace of the city where God has placed him.

views.view: Witness primarily through a distinct community, wary of the corruptions of power
views.body: This view holds that the church's primary political act is to be the church, a community whose shared life under Christ is itself a witness to a different kingdom, and it is wary of how readily engagement with power corrupts the engager. The model is the early church changing the world from below without holding any office, the martyrs whose refusal said more than any policy, the Anabaptist conviction that the kingdom of the cross must never wield the sword. Advocates argue that the church loses its soul every time it marries the power of its age, that the gospel advances by laid-down life and not seized control, and that the most political thing believers can do is form a contrast community the world cannot explain. They do not counsel total withdrawal, but they insist the church's distinctness must never be traded for a seat at the table. The danger they are guarding against is a church so absorbed in the contest for power that it becomes indistinguishable from a party, baptizing its sins and forfeiting the gospel to win an election. Against that they hold that the watching world is changed less by Christians who seize the levers than by Christians whose common life proves there is another King.

parts.title: What the Two Kingdoms Forms in You
parts.body:
You do not escape political idolatry by caring less about justice or by pretending to have no convictions. Indifference is not the goal, and detachment is not the gospel. God means to form a particular kind of citizen in the believer who learns to hold the two kingdoms rightly, and the forming is the point, because the public square is one more arena in which Christ remakes a person into his own image.

He forms freedom from fear. The believer whose hope is anchored in a kingdom that cannot be voted out is set free from the dread that owns the political animal, the terror of the wrong outcome, the conviction that everything rides on the next election. He can work hard for a just cause and lose without losing his world, because his world was secured at the cross and not at the ballot box. This freedom is not apathy. It is the calm of a person who has read the end of the story and knows which kingdom stands, and from that calm he can act with energy and without panic, which is exactly what the panicked public square most needs.

He forms a love that crosses the line. Political idolatry teaches you to hate the opponent, because if the tribe is ultimate then its enemies are your enemies. The two-kingdoms vision dissolves that hatred, because it tells you the person across the line is not finally your enemy but your neighbor, a fellow image-bearer for whom Christ died, and that your security does not depend on defeating him. The believer formed in this freedom can disagree without contempt, argue without dehumanizing, and lose without bitterness, because his identity was never staked on the win. He becomes, in a country drunk on contempt, a sober and startling thing, a person who can hold a conviction and a hand at the same time.

And he forms the courage to tell the truth to his own side. The deepest test of whether the faith owns the politics or the politics owns the faith is whether a believer can name the sins of his own tribe. The idolater excuses in his side what he condemns in the other, because the tribe is his god and a god can do no wrong. The believer set free by the two kingdoms can say the hard, costly word to the people whose approval he most wants, because he answers to a higher King than the crowd, and Christ has loosened the grip of his need to belong. This courage is rare and expensive. It will get you called a traitor by your own. But it is the mark of a person who finally has only one Lord, and it is the freedom that the watching world, exhausted by tribes that can do no wrong, is quietly desperate to see.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: Political sanity is not a position you adopt. It is a set of practices that slowly loosen the grip of the tribe and re-anchor the heart in the one Lord. None of what follows will solve the country's divisions, and none of it will purge the idol by Friday. All of it will start to wear a groove if you keep at it. Begin where you are, with one thing, this week.

steps: Notice your body when the news breaks. The dread, the vindication, the surge of contempt. Name it honestly as worship rather than citizenship, and bring the idol to God by name. You cannot repent of an allegiance you keep calling civic duty.

Pray for the leaders you did not vote for, by name, the way Scripture commands prayer for kings. Not that they would fail, but that God would grant them wisdom. Watch what blessing an opponent does to the heart that was learning to hate him.

Audit who is discipling you. Count the hours this week given to the voices of your tribe against the hours given to Scripture and the church, and adjust the ratio. You are being formed by whatever speaks to you most.
Say one true and costly thing about your own side. Name a sin your tribe excuses, out loud, to someone in it. Notice how hard it is, and let the difficulty show you how much the tribe already owns.

Read the render to Caesar passage and the trial before Pilate slowly, and ask where your tribe is asking for the worship that belongs to God alone. Draw the line Jesus drew, and keep it where he kept it.

Build one real friendship across the political line and refuse to let it become a debate. Know the person, hear why they believe what they believe, until the abstraction your tribe handed you breaks against a particular human face.

Practice losing well. Take one issue where your side did not prevail and choose to keep working, praying, and loving without despair, as proof to your own heart that your hope was never riding on the outcome.

Examine your church. Is its real unity in the blood of Christ or in a shared politics. Have one honest conversation about whether a believer who votes differently is fully welcome, fully a brother, fully at the table.

Engage the public square as a resident alien, seeking the welfare of the city through some concrete work for the common good, while guarding your heart against the idol that wants to ride along with the engagement.

Read the church under empire, the martyrs who would not burn the incense, Augustine on the two cities, the Confessing Church refusing to crown the nation. Let the long history teach you what captivity to power costs and what freedom from it looks like.

Hold your convictions and your charity together for a whole season, refusing to soften the truth and refusing to hate the opponent, until the watching people in your life see a believer who can do both, which almost no one in the country can.

Memorize the ancient creed until it governs your loyalties. Jesus is Lord, and Caesar is not. Let it sit over every election, every cause, every tribe, as the single sentence that orders all your lesser allegiances.

Build a life whose deepest community runs across the political lines, so that your friendships, your church, and your table are visibly wider than your party, a standing rebuke to a country that has made politics the measure of belonging.

Practice, over years, the long obedience of refusing the idol even when your side holds power and the temptation to baptize its every act is strongest. The test of faith in the public square is how you behave when you are winning.

Become a peacemaker between believers the tribes have divided, using whatever standing you have to remind the church that its unity was purchased by blood and is not for sale to any party. Refuse to let politics tear apart what the cross joined.

Keep returning to the King already enthroned. Read the gospel for the rest of your life not as a chaplain to your politics but as the rule over them, until your hope rests so fully in the kingdom that cannot be voted out that you become the freest person in the public square, owned by no tribe, terrified of no result, captive to no party, belonging only to him.
